title: Lumepay Raises $6M Pre-Seed to Scale African Cross-Border Payments
snippet: Lumepay has disclosed a $6 million pre-seed round to expand its cross-border payments and digital asset infrastructure across Africa, following regulatory clearance to enter Kenya. The post Lumepay Raises $6M Pre-Seed to Scale African Cross-Border Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
South African cross-border payments provider Lumepay has disclosed a $6 million pre-seed funding round backed by founder-led angels and domestic fintech investors. Closed at the start of 2026 alongside approximately $10 million in capital float secured to anchor client liquidity, the capital supports the company’s rail-agnostic B2B payments and digital asset infrastructure for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), corporates, and financial institutions.

The disclosure comes amid rapid structural shifts across global money movement, with worldwide cross-border payment volumes projected to reach $320 trillion by 2032. Across Africa, businesses are increasingly moving away from fragmented correspondent banking chains toward faster settlement networks—a trend underscored by transaction values on the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) more than doubling in 2026 compared to the prior year.

Multi-Rail Infrastructure and East African Expansion

Led by CEO Harry Huang, chief operating officer Luc Varejes, and chief legal and compliance officer Tatenda Nhemachena—who bring more than 20 years of combined industry experience alongside a broader executive team—Lumepay operates at the intersection of conventional banking rails, foreign exchange depth, and stablecoin liquidity.

Lumepay co-founders from left to right, COO, Luc Varejes, CEO Harry Huang, chief legal and compliance officer, Tatenda Nhemachena

Following the pre-seed close, the company executed several commercial rollouts across the continent:

Digital Asset Trading: Launched Lumetrade, its institutional digital asset and stablecoin trading venue, in April 2026.

Cross-Border Payments Platform: Rolled out its broader B2B cross-border payments platform across Africa in June 2026.

Kenyan Market Entry: Secured regulatory clearance from the Central Bank of Kenya in October 2026 to launch local operations, enabling Kenyan enterprises to settle international supplier invoices in currencies including Chinese yuan (CNY), US dollars (USD), and Indian rupees (INR) while executing intra-African transfers.

Lumepay and Lumetrade are currently live across the West African CFA franc zone (XOF), Central African CFA franc zone (XAF), Nigeria (NGN), Ghana (GHS), Tanzania (TZS), Malawi (MWK), Mozambique (MZN), and Kenya (KES), with additional regulatory approvals pending to expand local payment capabilities. Looking ahead, the firm is prioritizing expansion across Southern, West, and Central Africa, specifically targeting Malawi, Mozambique, and the XOF and XAF regions.

“The future of cross-border payments isn’t traditional finance or stablecoins; it’s a combination of both, backed by the FX depth to make them work for real businesses,” stated Harry Huang. “That’s how we’ve built Lumepay: a rail-agnostic platform that works at the intersection between the two… Our integrated approach addresses the real drivers of friction: fragmentation, liquidity inefficiency and execution risk.”

“In the months since the raise, we’ve turned plans into working products: diversified and reliable liquidity; a platform that handles cross-border payments end to end; a growing network of partners and payment rails; and regulatory clearance in South Africa and Kenya, together with licensed partners across Francophone West and Central Africa,” added Luc Varejes.

Tier-One Banking Partnerships and Regulatory Architecture

To support institutional transaction volumes, Lumepay has established direct banking and regulatory infrastructure across key jurisdictions:

South African Payment Rails: Lumepay (Pty) Ltd operates as a registered Third-Party Payment Provider (TPPP) in South Africa, partnering with Nedbank as its sponsoring bank for domestic rand (ZAR) merchant collections and disbursements.

Regulated Digital Asset Dealing: Lume Trade (Pty) Ltd holds a Category I Financial Services Provider (FSP No. 54670) license covering intermediary services in crypto assets, derivatives, and deposits, utilizing a banking relationship with Standard Bank to facilitate ZAR deposits and withdrawals for institutional clients.

North American Registrations: Lumepay Limited is registered with Canada’s FINTRAC as a Money Services Business (MSB) and with the Bank of Canada as a payment service provider under the Retail Payment Activities Act.

“Banks are rigorous about who they work with, and they should be,” noted Tatenda Nhemachena. “Working with Nedbank and Standard Bank across our two businesses reflects the compliance standards we have built from day one.”

Having deployed its pre-seed capital to establish enterprise-grade security, wallet infrastructure, banking relationships, and licensed regional partnerships, Lumepay is now entering its growth phase and laying the groundwork for a Series A round.

title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Vertice Launches Procure-to-Pay to Close Post-Contract Value Leak
snippet: The London AI procurement platform says its new P2P module targets the 10%-plus of contract value that leaks after signing through missed discounts and The post Vertice Launches Procure-to-Pay to Close Post-Contract Value Leak appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Vertice, the London-based AI procurement platform, has launched a Procure-to-Pay (P2P) capability that extends its existing Intake-to-Procure product into invoice processing, purchase-order matching, spend controls and supplier payments. The company says the move creates a single record spanning every stage from initial purchase request to final settlement, giving finance and accounts payable teams unified visibility over data that is typically scattered across multiple systems.

The launch targets a specific and quantifiable inefficiency. According to a January 2026 report by World Commerce and Contracting, companies on average lose more than 11% of contract value after the deal is signed, through missed early-payment discounts and payment terms that drift in favour of the supplier. Vertice claims that customers running suppliers through the new P2P module have already unlocked faster payment cycles, better terms or improved cost forecasts for more than 80% of those relationships.

What the platform does

Eldar Tuvey, co-founder and CEO at Vertice

The intelligence layer underpinning the P2P module is Vertice’s proprietary spend dataset, which the company describes as covering $75 billion of processed spend across 32,000 vendors. The dataset is used to contextualise each invoice and contract against live market pricing, helping finance teams assess whether the terms they negotiated remain competitive and where a supplier is likely to accept renegotiation. AI agents handle the operational layer: classifying invoices, extracting data, reconciling against purchase orders and contract terms, and appending general-ledger codes and audit trails.

Eldar Tuvey, chief executive and co-founder of Vertice, said the core problem is one of visibility. “Finance teams can’t protect value if all they can see is a PO and an invoice,” he said. “We are giving Finance the visibility, context and automation they need to easily plug these leaks.”

Patrick Reymann, research director for procurement applications and agents at IDC, said extending the dataset to the payment layer was a logical progression from Vertice’s existing positioning. IDC named Vertice a Leader in its 2026 MarketScape for worldwide AI-enabled spend orchestration.

Market context

The procure-to-pay software market is well-populated. Established enterprise resource planning vendors bundle P2P modules as part of broader finance suites, while dedicated procurement platforms including Coupa, Ivalua and Zip have competed on workflow automation and supplier network depth. The differentiator Vertice is staking is the proprietary benchmark dataset: the argument is that knowing what other buyers pay the same vendor is worth more than workflow automation alone, because it shifts the negotiating posture rather than merely streamlining the paperwork.

That claim is plausible but depends on dataset quality, coverage breadth and recency, none of which Vertice has opened to independent audit. The 80% supplier improvement figure is an early-customer metric rather than a controlled study, and the absence of a defined baseline makes it difficult to assess. Buyers evaluating the platform will want to understand the vendor coverage within their own spend categories before committing.

The commercial case is sharpened by the current macro environment. With borrowing costs still elevated relative to the pre-2022 cycle, treasury and procurement teams are under pressure to optimise working capital actively rather than passively. Early-payment discount capture and dynamic payment-term management are straightforward levers, and automating them at the invoice level removes the manual reconciliation overhead that typically prevents finance teams from acting on them at scale.

Named customers including ARM, Brex, Duolingo, Twilio and Santander lend credibility to the enterprise positioning. The Financial Times recognised Vertice as the UK’s fastest-growing scale-up, though the criteria and year of that designation were not specified in the release. Vertice operates across six offices including New York, Sydney and Johannesburg, and says its platform is used in more than 100 countries. Procure-to-Pay is available immediately as part of the core platform.

title: Mercuryo Launches Swaps with 1,400 Routes Across 24 Digital Tokens
snippet: Mercuryo's new Swaps product offers fixed-quote token conversion across 24 assets and 21 blockchain networks, though it is unavailable in the US, UK The post Mercuryo Launches Swaps with 1,400 Routes Across 24 Digital Tokens appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mercuryo, the London-headquartered payments infrastructure platform, has launched Swaps, a token conversion product that lets users move holdings between 24 digital assets across 21 blockchain networks. The company says the product covers 1,400 distinct swap routes, offers fixed quotes and zero slippage, and is executable in a single click.

The asset list runs from the major tokens by market capitalisation, including bitcoin (BTC), ether (ETH) and the two dominant stablecoins, Tether’s USDt and USDC, through to more speculative names including Dogecoin, Pepe, Shiba Inu and Kaspa. Supported networks include Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, TON and the XRP Ledger, among others. Liquidity is sourced through an unnamed cryptocurrency exchange that Mercuryo says applies anti-money-laundering controls, though the company has not disclosed the counterparty.

The geographic restriction

The most commercially significant detail in the announcement is a geographic carve-out: Swaps is not available to users in the United States, the United Kingdom or the European Economic Area. That restriction covers the three largest regulated digital-asset markets by institutional participation and removes a substantial proportion of global retail trading volume from Mercuryo’s addressable user base for this product.

The exclusion is likely a regulatory precaution rather than a commercial choice. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority requires cryptoasset businesses to register and applies financial promotions rules that constrain how token conversion services can be marketed. Across the EEA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation (MiCA), which came fully into force in late 2024, creates a harmonised but demanding licensing and disclosure framework for crypto-asset service providers. The US remains fragmented across Securities and Exchange Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission and state-level money-transmission regimes, and enforcement actions against token swap venues have put overseas providers on notice. Rather than clear those hurdles immediately, Mercuryo appears to be launching in markets where the compliance overhead is lower, keeping its options open for regulated-market entry at a later stage.

Market context

Arthur Firstov, chief business officer at Mercuryo

Arthur Firstov, Mercuryo’s chief business officer, pointed to the company’s own on-ramp transaction data as the commercial rationale for the product. Mercuryo’s figures for the first half of 2026 show stablecoin transactions rising from 43 per cent to 60 per cent of total on-ramp volume during a period when bitcoin fell 33.2 per cent and ether dropped 47.3 per cent. The company interprets this as evidence that retail users are actively managing portfolio exposure rather than passively holding, creating demand for a low-friction conversion tool.

The token swap segment is well-established. Decentralised exchanges such as Uniswap and centralised platforms including Binance Convert and Coinbase‘s Simple Trade all offer similar functionality, often with broader asset coverage and deeper liquidity. Mercuryo’s proposition is the fixed-quote model, which removes slippage uncertainty at the cost of locking in a spread, and integration with its existing on-ramp and payment infrastructure for users already on the platform. Whether that bundled positioning is sufficient to attract meaningful volume outside the UK, US and EEA remains to be tested.

The company counts Trust Wallet, MetaMask, Revolut, Mastercard and Visa among its partners, which gives it distribution into existing user bases that could provide an early adoption channel for Swaps. The unnamed liquidity provider and the lack of any disclosed fee or spread structure are gaps that institutional observers will note before assessing the product’s competitiveness.

title: Mojo Mortgages: Income Caps will Block 13% from ‘Your First Home’
snippet: Data from Mojo Mortgages shows proposed household income limits will exclude over 13% of first-time buyer applicants nationally, rising to 22% in London. The post Mojo Mortgages: Income Caps will Block 13% from ‘Your First Home’ appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Andy Burnham‘s proposed ‘Your First Home’ scheme aims to cut the minimum deposit for first-time buyers to 2.5%, backed by a government equity loan covering 20% of the purchase price. New data from online mortgage broker Mojo Mortgages suggests the scheme’s income eligibility rules will bar a significant portion of the buyers it was designed to help.

John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages

According to Mojo’s internal customer data, the proposed household income caps of £90,000 outside London and £110,000 within Greater London would exclude more than 13% of first-time buyer applicants nationwide. In London and the surrounding area, that figure climbs to over 22%. The disproportionate impact on dual-earner couples in high-cost cities is the central tension the broker’s analysis highlights: two people each earning average London wages can easily clear the £110,000 threshold while still lacking sufficient savings to fund a conventional deposit.

John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages, said: “Lowering the deposit barrier to 2.5% addresses one of the single biggest hurdles first-time buyers face. However, introducing strict household income caps creates a delicate balancing act. Two average working earners buying together, especially in high-cost regions, can easily cross these thresholds, effectively locking out working couples who are already squeezed by high property values.”

The savings landscape behind the numbers

The same data set illustrates how first-time buyers are already adapting to structural affordability pressures. A Mojo Mortgages survey conducted by Censuswide in April 2026, covering 1,000 UK first-time buyers, found that 64% rely on side hustles such as resale platforms or freelance income to build their deposit savings, with 53% of that cohort reporting the additional income shortened their savings timeline by two to three years. A further 22% said they had remained in roles they described as toxic solely to maintain the income stability required for a mortgage application. Some 26% still relied on a gifted family deposit to complete a purchase.

Five schemes, five trade-offs

The release accompanies a full breakdown of the five current or proposed government-backed routes to homeownership. Beyond ‘Your First Home’, the active options include the Lifetime ISA, which offers a 25% government bonus on savings up to £4,000 per tax year but is capped at properties priced below £450,000; the First Homes Scheme, which provides a 30% to 50% discount on new-build properties for local key workers but suffers from severely constrained availability; the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme, which enables 95% LTV borrowing on open-market properties but at higher interest rates; and Shared Ownership, which calculates the deposit against a purchased share rather than full property value but layers in ongoing rent and service charges on top of mortgage payments.

Market context

The broader proptech and mortgage-fintech market has seen a wave of digital broker services competing on speed of comparison and the quality of eligibility tooling. Mojo, which compares products from more than 60 lenders, sits in a segment that includes Habito and Trussle. The commercial value of this kind of analysis is partly editorial, establishing the broker as the authoritative voice on scheme eligibility, and partly lead generation, the release closes with a prompt to consult a Mojo adviser.

The policy stakes are real, however. The interaction between income caps and property prices in London has been a recurring failure mode for previous help-to-buy iterations. Policymakers drafting the final ‘Your First Home’ legislation will need to determine whether the income thresholds should be indexed to regional property price-to-income ratios rather than set as fixed nominal figures. If they are not adjusted, the scheme risks replicating the geographic inequity of its predecessors even before a single mortgage is drawn down.

title: i2c Reports 42% Client Renewal Growth as PowerOne Scales Globally
snippet: The Redwood City payments processor added clients across banking, crypto and gaming while processing over $70bn in annual transaction volume. The post i2c Reports 42% Client Renewal Growth as PowerOne Scales Globally appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
i2c Inc. has published a year-in-review summary for its PowerOne unified banking and payments platform, citing a 42% rise in clients that renewed or expanded their programmes over two years and a 46% growth in its largest client portfolios over the same period. The Redwood City, California-based company processes more than $70 billion in annual transaction volume across 216 markets and claims 99.999% historical platform availability.

The announcement is framed around a wave of new client wins rather than a specific deal or funding event. Named additions span regulated banks, digital-asset firms and gaming-payments operators: Crypto.com extended its global card programme across dozens of markets without building new infrastructure; Belize Bank migrated its Mastercard and Visa portfolios onto PowerOne without service interruption; and Sightline Payments, working alongside Cross River Bank, used the platform to launch what it described as a first-of-its-kind payments ecosystem for the US gaming industry. Latin American digital bank Inter also joined the client roster to support international expansion, and Wealthsimple, one of Canada’s larger fintech platforms, cited the platform’s configurability as a key factor in its partnership.

Platform architecture as the competitive argument

Amir Wain, CEO at i2c Inc.

The commercial thesis i2c is advancing is one shared by a small number of global card-processing vendors: that a single, unified technology stack outperforms stitched-together multi-vendor arrangements on reliability, speed of product configuration, and total cost of ownership. The company claims more than 300 APIs, more than 100,000 pre-coded building blocks, and 1.5 million engineering hours invested annually in continuous development, with 30% of its workforce dedicated to research and development.

That argument has gained traction partly because the alternative is genuinely painful. New American Banker research, conducted in partnership with i2c, found that 88% of financial institutions have accelerated their modernisation timelines in response to competition from digital-first banks and non-bank providers, with legacy processing architecture cited most often as the primary barrier. The tension between proven scale on old infrastructure and agility on modern stacks is a real operational dilemma, and it shapes purchasing decisions at the programme manager and chief technology officer level.

Founder and chief executive Amir Wain described the platform’s direction in terms that signal a move toward agentic AI capabilities, framing unified data and decisioning workflows as the prerequisite architecture. “Our work toward agentic AI builds on the advantage of unified data, workflows, and decisioning, creating a foundation where intelligence can operate across the platform rather than being bolted onto fragmented systems,” he said.

Market context and competitive landscape

The card-issuing and processing segment is consolidating around a handful of global platforms. i2c competes against processors with significantly larger balance sheets, including Marqeta, Galileo (now part of SoFi), and established network-affiliated processing arms. Differentiation in this space tends to come from configurability, speed to market for new card programmes, and the depth of support for non-standard use cases such as multi-currency prepaid, crypto-linked debit and gaming wallets. The Sightline and CoinZoom client wins suggest i2c is deliberately targeting these higher-complexity, higher-margin niches rather than competing on volume alone.

Industry recognition during the year included placement in IDC FinTech Rankings’ Top 100, a Leading Vendor designation from Celent in card issuing and processing, and Established Leader status in Juniper Research‘s Modern Card Issuing Platforms Market 2025-2030 report. The company also joined Mastercard’s Crypto Partner Program and the Open Standard USD initiative, signalling ambition in stablecoin payment infrastructure.

i2c also made several senior leadership appointments, including a new chief financial officer, chief revenue officer, chief marketing officer and general counsel, suggesting the company is building out the executive layer typically associated with a business preparing for a liquidity event or a significant expansion phase, though no such plans were disclosed in the release.

title: Neovision Launches ADGM Feeder Fund for UAE Retail Indian Equity Access
snippet: Neovision Wealth Management has opened the DSP Equity Opportunities Feeder Fund PC to UAE retail investors from $100, removing most legacy NRI onboarding steps. The post Neovision Launches ADGM Feeder Fund for UAE Retail Indian Equity Access appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Neovision Wealth Management has launched the DSP Equity Opportunities Feeder Fund PC in the Abu Dhabi Global Market, giving eligible investors in the UAE dollar-denominated access to Indian listed equities from a minimum of $100. The fund is registered with the FSRA as a Public Fund, a Feeder Fund and a Passported Fund, allowing it to be offered to retail investors onshore in the UAE through licensed promoters.

The structure feeds into the Direct Plan Growth Option of the DSP Large & Mid Cap Fund, managed by DSP Asset Managers’ portfolio team under lead portfolio manager Rohit Singhania. Investor onboarding, transaction processing and portfolio tracking are handled digitally through Valura.AI, which holds a UAE distribution licence.

Removing friction for NRI investors

Ashish Marwah, director and chief investment officer at Neovision Wealth Management

For Indian professionals based in the UAE, the conventional route to Indian equity exposure has involved opening an NRE or NRO account, obtaining a Permanent Account Number, completing KYC with an Indian intermediary and converting funds into rupees, typically across multiple institutions and offline touchpoints. The feeder structure relocates most of that burden to the fund itself: the vehicle is registered to invest in India, so currency conversion and Indian regulatory compliance happen at the fund level rather than at the investor level. Investors hold a US dollar share class and do not need an Indian bank account or PAN to subscribe.

Ashish Marwah, director and chief investment officer of Neovision Wealth Management and the ADGM fund manager, was clear that the dollar wrapper removes the conversion step, not the currency risk. “A US dollar share class removes the conversion step, not the currency risk,” he said. The fund does not hedge its rupee exposure, so dollar returns move with the INR/USD rate.

Structure, costs and the retail economics

The fund operates two share classes. The retail Class R carries a management fee of 1.50% per annum with total annual fund expenses capped at 1.80% of NAV. The institutional Class I carries a $500,000 minimum. Expenses of the underlying DSP fund are borne by the feeder proportionately, outside the cap. The daily dealing structure, mirroring the underlying fund’s liquidity terms, spreads fixed administrative costs across all investors, which is what makes the $100 floor commercially viable at scale.

Eligibility is restricted to investors outside India. The digital onboarding process applies eligibility and AML checks at the point of entry, with manual review reserved for enhanced due diligence cases. Investors provide tax residency self-certifications to support FATCA and CRS reporting obligations.

The fund is a protected cell of DSP Funds (OEIC) PCC PLC. That architecture allows further cells, each with segregated assets and a distinct strategy, to be added under the same ADGM registration and digital distribution model. Marwah indicated that Neovision is in active growth, with ambitions to extend access to public markets, private markets and hard assets through additional licensed distributors.

Regulatory and market context

ADGM has emerged as the preferred domicile for a growing cohort of cross-border fund managers targeting Gulf-based investors. Its FSRA regulator is an IOSCO member and applies English common law directly, making it legible to international institutional counterparties. A passported fund registered with the FSRA can be promoted across the UAE onshore market, including to retail investors, which is not possible for funds domiciled outside the UAE. That structural advantage over distributing an existing offshore vehicle is a significant driver of the ADGM-feeder model.

The launch follows Neovision’s 2024 tokenisation of a T-bill fund in ADGM, which the firm has characterised as a first for the jurisdiction. The Indian equity fund represents a different regulatory and commercial proposition: a retail-accessible, daily-dealing vehicle built on conventional fund law rather than distributed ledger infrastructure.

title: Behind the Idea: Redvest
snippet: Redvest founder Anya Ozmen on building a game that teaches beginners to invest, the pivot from an AI trader and the brokerage partnerships ahead. The post Behind the Idea: Redvest appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Most people who start investing do it with real money and very little preparation. Redvest, a US gamified financial education platform, wants beginners to learn first: its app and website teach investing through games, quizzes, courses and competitions, then let users practise in a real-time stock market simulator using virtual money. The company says it has more than one million users across more than 40 countries.

Anya Ozmen, founder of Redvest

Its founder, Anya Ozmen, is a self-taught programmer who moved to the US from Turkey at 18 and built most of the product herself. In this Behind the Idea, she explains how an AI trading app turned down by the App Store became a learning platform, what growing it as a solo founder was like, and where Redvest goes next. The profit figures she gives for Redvest users are simulator results, made with virtual money rather than real trades.

Tell us more about your company and its offering

Redvest is a gamified financial education platform. Over 1 million Redvest users learn investing and finance with AI-powered games, competitions, courses and quizzes. Redvesters from 40+ countries have completed over 38,000 quizzes and generated over $500 million in order volume in the real-time stock market game. Our mission is to democratise access to financial education and empower Gen Zers to learn effectively by playing games, just like they did when they were kids!

What problem was your company set up to solve?

Around 80 per cent of retail investors lose money in the stock market, but 69 per cent to 83 per cent of Redvest users are profitable on our platform at any given time. Investing is easy, but making money is hard. Anyone can download Robinhood or Fidelity, but the majority lose money investing in the market, leaving them demotivated and one step behind on their financial journey. Redvest sets out to solve this problem by offering a risk-free, hands-on experience with AI-powered and data-driven gamified learning.

Since launch, how has your company evolved?

I built Redvest as an AI robo-adviser at first, as a fun side project when I was 23. It would automatically trade for you once you connected your brokerage account, using methods like value investing, technical trading and sentiment analysis according to your preferences and goals. When I submitted the app to the App Store, Apple actually didn’t accept it, so I ended up adding a stock market simulator to the platform to get it live on the App Store. However, when I put the app out there, I saw that people had a huge need for the learning piece. Users were completely lost about where to begin. They wanted to be able to control their trades, and no one was using the AI trader. All the attention was on the stock market simulator instead.

We pivoted to focusing on what our users needed and wanted the most. A couple of years later, we expanded to the web in addition to mobile and became the Duolingo of investing.

What has been the biggest challenge or most ‘tricky moment’ to overcome?

As a solo founder and self-taught developer, handling the initial growth was genuinely hard. In 2020, I started an AI software and mobile app development company, and through my work there, I taught myself how to program in a bunch of programming languages to help my team deliver client projects faster. I built and designed most of Redvest myself. It wasn’t as easy to build apps back then, and it took a lot longer to iterate. You needed to hand code all lines. There would be a bug, and I would stay up all night trying to fix it by myself without anyone to ask for advice. This taught me how to find and create resources for other people who might not have access to tools, information and large networks.

What are your biggest achievements or ‘proudest moment’ so far?

I’m proudest when we get an email from a customer about their positive experience, especially if it’s coupled with a new feature request! One specific moment of joy carved in my memory is when Redvest made the Top 30 for iOS in the Finance category. I saw Redvest’s logo next to big fintech companies’ logos, and I teared up. Having built most of the app and the website myself, it felt like seeing my kid graduate. I grew up in Turkey until I was 18, and my world was very small. I had never dreamt of anything big like this.

How would you describe the culture of your company?

Redvest’s company culture is focused on positivity and problem-solving. Our mission is to create tools that help and teach people while entertaining them, so the same applies to our team. Our team mostly consists of recent college graduates. My personal mission is to teach them as much as I can, setting them up for success in their career journeys. Most Fridays, we have a game hour as a team, playing games like Codenames, Pictionary and more!

What’s in store for the future?

Currently, we are working on some new and exciting partnerships with brokerages to bring educational tools to their platforms so that consumers coming to invest on those platforms can set themselves up for success.

title: Aldar and ADIB Launch Co-Branded Darna Covered Cards in Abu Dhabi
snippet: Aldar and ADIB have launched two Visa co-branded cards tied to the Darna loyalty programme, offering up to 10% back on retail and hospitality The post Aldar and ADIB Launch Co-Branded Darna Covered Cards in Abu Dhabi appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Aldar Properties and Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank (ADIB) have jointly launched a pair of co-branded covered cards linked to Aldar’s Darna digital loyalty programme, deepening the intersection of property, retail and Islamic banking in Abu Dhabi’s consumer market.

The two products, the ADIB Aldar Visa Infinite and the ADIB Aldar Visa Platinum Covered Cards, were issued on 21 October 2026. Both sit inside the Live Aldar app ecosystem, allowing cardholders to earn, track and redeem Darna Points across Aldar’s retail, hospitality, education and residential portfolio.

The product structure

The reward tiers are graduated. Cardholders earn up to 10% value back in Darna Points on eligible spending at participating Aldar malls, hotels, golf courses, restaurants and entertainment venues. Spending on Aldar property purchases and Aldar Education attracts up to 1.5%, while eligible international transactions earn up to 2%. Welcome bonuses of up to 20,000 Darna Points, equivalent to AED 1,000, are offered on sign-up, subject to card tier and qualifying conditions.

Additional benefits include complimentary Darna Gold or Platinum status depending on tier, access to more than 1,000 airport lounges worldwide, complimentary valet parking up to four times per month at selected UAE locations, and an annual fee waiver from the second year onwards for cardholders who meet defined spend thresholds: AED 30,000 in foreign currency or AED 75,000 in total transactions.

Faisal Falaknaz, group chief financial and sustainability officer at Aldar, said the partnership extends rewards to eligible property spend, “creating meaningful value around one of our customers’ most significant purchases.” Amit Malhotra, global head of retail banking at ADIB, framed the proposition as embedding banking more deeply into customers’ daily lives beyond traditional service relationships.

The cards are Sharia-compliant covered structures rather than conventional credit products, consistent with ADIB’s Islamic banking model. ADIB reported total assets of AED 304 billion as of June 2026, giving the partnership institutional weight within the UAE’s Islamic finance sector.

Market context and regulatory landscape

The co-branded card space in the Gulf has grown steadily as banks seek to deepen primary-account relationships and retailers look to translate loyalty programmes into payment data. The Aldar-ADIB structure is notable for spanning property purchasing alongside everyday retail, a combination that is less common than pure lifestyle or travel reward cards. Rewarding property transactions at the card level blurs the boundary between mortgage product and payment card, a wrinkle that sits within the DFSA and CBUAE regulatory perimeter for consumer credit and Islamic finance structures.

Visa’s involvement as the network rail gives the product global acceptance infrastructure, but the commercial logic is primarily domestic. Abu Dhabi’s real estate market has remained buoyant through 2025 and into 2026, driven by continued government investment and population growth, which provides a large addressable base for property-linked financial products.

Several UAE banks and property groups have experimented with similar closed-loop loyalty integrations, but the scale of Aldar’s landbank, which spans 76 million square metres, and the breadth of the Live Aldar app ecosystem give this proposition a wider earn-and-redeem surface than most comparable products in the region.

The near-term test for the partnership will be activation rates and whether the Live Aldar app can sustain engagement outside of property transaction moments. Loyalty programmes anchored to infrequent, high-value purchases, such as property, tend to require a rich everyday-spend layer to maintain cardholder relevance, which the retail and hospitality reward tiers are designed to provide.

title: Arf and Ripple Bring RLUSD Settlement Liquidity to XRPL
snippet: Swiss-regulated Arf will supply short-duration working capital in RLUSD to licensed cross-border payment firms settling on the XRP Ledger. The post Arf and Ripple Bring RLUSD Settlement Liquidity to XRPL appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Arf, a Swiss-regulated financial institution headquartered in Zug, has partnered with Ripple to deliver stablecoin-denominated settlement liquidity to licensed cross-border payment companies operating on the XRP Ledger (XRPL). The arrangement uses Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin as the working capital instrument and targets a structural problem that has dogged the cross-border payments industry for years: the timing mismatch between when a payment company must fund a transaction and when the underlying settlement actually arrives.

Arf reported that it has scaled to roughly $10 billion in annual global settlement volume since launching in November 2022, with capital turning over approximately four times a month. That velocity matters commercially: short-duration, high-turnover liquidity looks very different on a balance sheet and in a regulatory capital calculation than a traditional revolving credit line, which can take months to establish and typically demands collateral pledged in a single jurisdiction. For payment companies whose working capital needs to move across markets in step with payment flows, that mismatch is the core operational constraint the partnership is designed to address.

How the facility works

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO at Arf

In the first phase, Arf will provide RLUSD liquidity directly on XRPL. Drawdowns are expected to be repaid within one to five business days as cross-border payments settle, allowing the same pool of capital to be recycled repeatedly against live payment flows. Arf retains underwriting and working capital decisions offchain, while XRPL provides the settlement rail.

A second phase is contingent on XRPL’s native lending infrastructure becoming operational. Once available, Arf says it intends to migrate more of its liquidity activity onto the protocol itself, enabling onchain capital management alongside its existing regulated treasury functions. No timeline for that infrastructure milestone was disclosed in the announcement.

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and chief executive of Arf, said the company is “meeting that need at scale, with $10 billion in annual settlement volume and capital turning over four times a month,” adding that the Ripple partnership is designed to help payment companies “bridge that gap and support more payment volume.”

Market and regulatory context

The announcement sits within the broader PayFi category, a term used to describe financial products structured around real-time payment flows and the time value of money, spanning settlement liquidity, receivables financing and fiat-to-stablecoin treasury management. Arf and Huma Finance are credited with coining the category; the partnership with Ripple extends Arf’s regulated infrastructure into a public blockchain environment.

RLUSD, Ripple’s dollar stablecoin, launched in late 2024 and is positioned as a regulated instrument for institutional settlement use cases rather than retail trading. Stablecoins used in payment settlement are increasingly subject to regulatory attention on both sides of the Atlantic. In the EU, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation covers asset-referenced and e-money tokens with specific capital and reserve requirements; in the UK, the Payment and Electronic Money Institution Regulations and the FCA‘s evolving stablecoin framework will shape how arrangements of this kind are treated domestically. Arf’s Swiss regulatory status under VQF membership provides a foundation for cross-border operation, though each market in which its liquidity is deployed will carry its own licensing considerations.

For payment operators evaluating the proposition, the key variables are the cost of RLUSD-denominated liquidity relative to existing bank credit, the jurisdictional reach of the facility, and the operational risk profile of a settlement rail that is partly onchain. The transition to native XRPL lending infrastructure, when it arrives, will shift some of that risk profile further onto the protocol layer and will be the more consequential development to watch.

title: Interactive Brokers Launches Autonomous AI Trading Capability
snippet: IBKR Autonomous Trading lets eligible clients authorise connected AI to monitor and execute trades across 75,000+ listed instruments within a dedicated partition. The post Interactive Brokers Launches Autonomous AI Trading Capability appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Interactive Brokers (Nasdaq: IBKR) has launched IBKR Autonomous Trading, a capability that allows eligible clients to authorise connected AI platforms to monitor markets and submit orders on their behalf across more than 75,000 listed stocks, options and ETFs worldwide. 

The feature centres on a dedicated AI Partition, a ring-fenced allocation within a client’s existing IBKR account funded by internal transfer rather than a new account opening. Within that partition, a connected AI can monitor markets, evaluate opportunities against client-defined instructions and execute supported orders without requiring the client to approve each trade individually.

How the partition works

Clients configure the AI using natural language instructions. The examples Interactive Brokers published in its release cover a range of use cases: volatility screening at a set time of day, position-level drawdown alerts with options pricing context, automatic rebalancing when a holding breaches a portfolio-weight threshold, and covered-call writing triggered by implied volatility percentile. The firm says these parameters and account-level safeguards govern what the AI may and may not do.

IBKR already offered an AI Integration feature allowing clients to generate trade instructions for manual review and approval via platforms including ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Perplexity through Model Context Protocol connections. Autonomous Trading extends that by removing the per-order approval step for clients who meet eligibility requirements. The company said eligibility, funding limits and availability will vary by jurisdiction and IBKR affiliate; the capability is live across the US, UK, Europe, Singapore and Australia at launch.

Milan Galik, chief executive of Interactive Brokers, said the product builds on the firm’s longstanding automation philosophy: “IBKR Autonomous Trading builds on that approach, allowing clients to define their trading strategies and safeguards while connected AI monitors markets and executes trades within those parameters.”

Market and regulatory context

IBKR’s move sits inside a broader structural shift in which AI is being embedded at the execution layer of brokerage, not just the research or screening layer. Several algorithmic and quantitative platforms already offer automated strategy execution, but most are aimed at professional or institutional users. A product at a major retail-accessible broker that allows natural-language strategy definition represents a meaningful lowering of the barrier to AI-assisted autonomous execution for individual investors.

The regulatory picture is complicated and will determine how far the product can travel. In the UK, the FCA‘s Consumer Duty framework places responsibility on firms to ensure products are appropriate for the clients who use them, which will apply scrutiny to how IBKR determines eligibility and communicates risk. In the EU, MiFID II suitability obligations similarly govern algorithmic and automated order submission. In the US, the SEC and FINRA have both signalled heightened interest in AI-generated investment advice and automated order flow. IBKR has acknowledged country and entity eligibility restrictions, and the product’s trajectory in each jurisdiction will depend partly on how regulators treat the distinction between a client-configured instruction and a firm-provided recommendation.

The near-term questions for the market are the scale of the AI Partition funding caps at launch, the rate at which eligibility criteria are relaxed, and whether third-party AI providers beyond those already integrated will be able to connect to the framework.

title: Western Union, Intermex clash
snippet: The money transfer services company dropped its acquisition of the smaller rival after California regulators weighed in, but now a fight over the deal has ensued.
fullText:
Remittance services provider Western Union planned to buy International Money Express, but opted out Tuesday. Now, the two companies have begun a battle over whether the $500 million deal should be consummated.

Western Union had been waiting more than a year for regulators to approve a purchase of the younger rival also known as Intermex, but when the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation issued approval conditions Tuesday, the acquirer backed out. Western Union decided against the deal and notified Intermex it was terminating the acquisition agreement on Tuesday, the day that was the deadline for either side to exit the pact.

The California regulator “delivered unacceptable final Conditions of Approval that would have required material changes to Western Union’s business model, its agent relationships and execution of its long-term business strategy,” Western Union said in a press release late Tuesday. 

Western Union’s move isn’t passing muster with Intermex, which notified Western Union on Wednesday that it expects the transaction to be completed. Now, a legal fight is brewing.

“Through its counsel, Intermex has responded to Western Union rejecting Western Union's purported termination of the merger agreement and demanding that Western Union take all actions necessary to consummate the merger,” Intermex said in its statement.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, announced in August 2025 that it would purchase Intermex, but since then the companies have been trying to gather needed regulatory approvals. Miami-based Intermex was founded in 1994.

“Western Union stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and disagrees with Intermex’s characterization of the termination,” a spokesperson for Western Union said by email. “Western Union believes it acted in accordance with the terms of the agreement and will respond as appropriate.”

While New York regulators reached an agreement with the companies for approval of the deal earlier this year, the companies still needed California’s input, given the states’ purview over money transfer businesses.

The California agency approved the deal Tuesday, but imposed conditions that it said were aimed at safeguarding consumers, preventing fraud, deterring money laundering and ensuring “ fair and competitive access to financial services.”

California called Western Union a major money transfer company used by Californians to send money to Mexico and Central America, but it also noted that Intermex is a significant player in the market, saying the merger would have “significant implications for California consumers.” 

To consummate the merger, the state regulator said in a Tuesday statement that the companies must “take certain steps,” that it didn’t specify in its public statement, “to detect and deter fraud.” 

The regulator also prohibited the companies from reducing the number of agent locations that provide services in California.Citing an existing court order requiring Western Union to thwart criminal use of its network, the regulator also called on the company to “adopt robust risk-based anti-fraud and anti-money laundering measures.”

The state department also underscored its conditions with a threat. “If Western Union consummates its transaction with Intermex and fails to comply with these conditions, DFPI can take enforcement actions that may lead to limitations on its business practices or suspension of its license,” California’s statement said. 

The state noted federal immigration policies under the Trump administration have affected the market. That negative impact from reduced immigration movement that leads migrant workers to send money to friends and family was clear last week during Western Union’s third-quarter earnings report. 

“The last 18 months have been a difficult period for the remittance industry, particularly for those of us with relatively large retail franchises in the Americas,” Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan said during a webcast with analysts. “We have seen both an overall decline in the retail market and an acceleration of the shift towards digital.”

As part of its cost-cutting and shift to more digital operations, McGranahan said that Western Union had eliminated 500 full-time employees and has started a voluntary retirement program that it expects to lead to 150 more employee departures. 

At the end of last year, the company had about 9,600 workers worldwide, according to its annual filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
snippet: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.What firms need to do nowSo, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
snippet: A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers.
fullText:
Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles.

While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service.

A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter.

Ariel Nelson

Permission granted by National Consumer Law Center

The rise of these businesses is “really revealing in what they say about the state of affordability around life essentials,” said Ariel Nelson, a senior attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “These products are really appealing because people are desperate.”

Companies seeking to develop a market in the rental area include RealPage, an apartment management software firm, which last year bought Livble, a startup that offers renters flexible payment options. Another is New York-based Flexible Finance, known as Flex, which lets consumers split their rent, mortgage or other monthly bill payments. 

A third rent-focused fintech is Bilt Technologies, which offers a payments and loyalty program aimed at attracting rent and mortgage payments to credit cards, including its co-branded cards. In addition to points for rent and everyday spending on cards, New York-based Bilt issues points for homeowners’ association and condominium fee payments.

Bilt members can transfer the points to 18 airline and seven hotel loyalty partner programs to redeem for flights and hotel stays. The points can also be redeemed at merchants such as Amazon.com and Lyft.

Consumer advocates contend that pay-later products aimed at rent and medical care can exacerbate financial strains for economically vulnerable people and lead to a stacking of their debt.

“As the price of shelter has shot up, a new breed of predatory creditors has emerged aiming to turn this emergency into profit,” advocacy group Protect Borrowers said in a February report on the rent now, pay later industry. “Beneath the surface, these products are united in being little more than a repackaging of an age-old debt trap: payday loans.”

About 109 million Americans have a monthly rental payment, according to Protect Borrowers, a Washington-based nonprofit that lobbies and litigates on consumer debt issues. The group was formed in 2018 as the Student Borrower Protection Center by former officials of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. 

Pay-later options allow renters to avoid being late on their rent, avoiding landlords’ late fees and revolving credit card interest rates that can reach 30% or more, Zahir Khoja, RealPage’s chief fintech officer, said in an interview last month. The average late fee is $85, he said.

“It’s not that you can’t pay your rent,” he said of tenant customers that select pay-later plans. “You may not be able to pay your rent on January 1st, and so you need some time in the month of January to be able to do it. It’s much better than paying a late fee or revolving at 29.9 (percent) on credit.”

Another BNPL provider, Sydney-based Zip, offers a bill-payment service to split monthly bills such as insurance, utilities and mobile phone. The company is also exploring a new rent-focused service for the U.S. market. 

Many “everyday Americans” are challenged by a misalignment between the timing of their income and bills, Zip’s former U.S. CEO, Joe Heck, told analysts on the BNPL provider’s August earnings call. Heck left Zip last month, the company said in an Oct. 16 investor announcement.

“Most consumers are paid every two weeks, while bills like rent are generally due monthly,” Heck said. “That mismatch in timing of income and expenses creates large opportunities beyond BNPL,” he said, pointing to bill payments and the need for “income-smoothing” as other ways the services could be used. 

Shragie Lichtenstein

Permission granted by Flex

The U.S. monthly rent and bill market is a $2 trillion addressable opportunity, compared to $160 billion for the retail BNPL market, Zip said in its investor presentation.

“I do think that this is a trend, both for rent and in general consumer essentials, that’s likely to continue,” Flex co-founder and CEO Shragie Lichtenstein said in an interview Oct. 8. 

Competing payment plans

RealPage, which is based in suburban Dallas, sells property-management software and rent payment financing services. The company offers both Livble and Flex via its app for residents and property managers or owners. 

Despite its Livble ownership, RealPage promotes both brands with its property owner customers, Khoja said. “We tell them ‘Hey, it’s Pepsi (or) Coke. Let the customer decide which one works for them.’”

Flex is a subscription service for tenants that collects a percentage of the rent as a payment for the service, he said Oct. 18, during an interview at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. “Whereas ours (Livble) is just a flat fee, so it’s different – whatever works for you better as the resident.”

Another difference is that Flex offers credit cards as a payment method, while Livble accepts only ACH, said Khoja, who joined RealPage in March. 

Livble charges customers a fee for each payment they make, eschewing recurring monthly membership or subscription fees. Livble’s typical payment fee is $30 to $35 but are “nuanced by state,” which is why they’re not posted on the company’s website, a RealPage spokesperson said last week in an email. A resident using Livble, “will always know the fee before it’s final,” the spokesperson said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a question about how it presents its fees to customers. 

“We don’t want you to get into perpetual debt,” Khoja said. “Our goal is to actually help you go up the financial-inclusion ladder, where you’re now able to stand on your own two feet and do things without revolving credit at such high rates or taking third-party loans that you can’t repay.”

A playground at an apartment complex in Irving, Texas, near Dallas.

Getty Images

Two years ago, the Justice Department and eight states filed an antitrust lawsuit alleging that RealPage helped apartment owners collude to fix rental prices. The lawsuit said that the company’s pricing software used nonpublic, sensitive data collected from apartment owners to develop rental rate recommendations in various markets and keep rents higher than they would have been in a competitive market.

The company and government settled the case last year, with RealPage agreeing to stop using sensitive information from landlords to determine the rental prices that it suggested through its software. The company did not admit or deny wrongdoing or face a financial penalty as part of the agreement. Several antitrust lawsuits filed by states and private plaintiffs continue. Private equity firm Thoma Bravo acquired RealPage in 2021. 

Another rent-payment focused startup, New York-based Esusu, has partnered with BNPL provider Affirm Holdings to allow renters to split their rent into two equal payments. The Esusu program remains an “early-stage pilot” in testing and consists only of evenly split rent payments, with no fees or interest, an Affirm spokesperson said last month in an email.

Esusu charges a $59 membership fee, paid monthly or annually, depending on whether a tenant’s apartment property is part of the company’s network. The company also has a “split pay” program allowing renters to pay 60% of their rent upfront and divide the remainder into two or three payments. Esusu did not respond to a message seeking comment on its business model. 

Determining the costs of these rent-payment programs “can be confusing,” said Nelson, the NCLC attorney, noting that such information is often buried deep within user terms and conditions.

“I cannot for the life of me figure out how much they cost,” she said of having looked around different pay-later providers’ websites for pricing information. “And that’s also a problem.”

Scattered regulatory oversight

Pay-later lending has had little oversight at the federal level. Several states – including Illinois, New York and Oregon – have formulated rules to regulate the industry as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has contracted during the Trump administration. 

In June, U.S. Rep. Daniel Goldman, a Democrat from New York City, introduced a bill to apply the federal Truth in Lending Act to BNPL loans, effectively regulating them as credit cards. The measure hasn’t moved beyond the House Financial Services Committee, according to Congress’ website.

BNPL “users have been left with no federal protections,” Goldman said in a press release announcing his bill, referring to the CFPB’s decision to retreat last year from a 2024 decision to regulate pay-later loans much like credit cards.

Another bill, filed by Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat, would amend the Truth in Lending law, which dates to the late 1960s, and the 2010 Consumer Financial Protection Act to apply new oversight and consumer protections. Reed’s legislation, filed late last year, has attracted four Democratic co-sponsors and a companion bill in the House, but no Republican sponsors, according to Congress.gov.

Lichtenstein, the Flex CEO, said that one challenge facing the RNPL industry is that these products “don’t fit into a clean box” neatly for regulators to evaluate what they are and how they work.

“The more you don’t fit into a clean box, the more regulatory scrutiny it draws,” he said. “We have tried our best to fit into a relatively clean box,” he said, adding that the company has “internal guardrails” to help it evaluate “the many, many gray areas that can exist for consumer fintech.”

However, he added, pay-later services for rent differ from other financial services, often “embedded” with the rent payment and with different pricing models. 

The RNPL industry doesn’t currently have a “uniform set of standards” from regulators under which to operate, Lichtenstein said, which can lead to different practices among the various players. “Continued clarity on the right way to do things would be welcome by us,” he said.

Risks for renters?

Beyond high fees and the potential for debt accumulation, rent-payment services pose “a significant risk” to borrowers because lenders often link directly to consumers’ bank accounts and offer “disastrously poor customer service” in addressing errors or other account issues, according to the Protect Borrowers report. 

Their growth is also likely to lead to further regulatory scrutiny, with at least one state, New York, being encouraged by the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to apply its BNPL rules expansively to other providers in adjacent verticals. 

Pay-later services are marketed by lenders “who claim that these loans can ease the housing affordability or healthcare accessibility crisis,” Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine of the New York City DCWP wrote in September in a letter to New York state financial regulators. “However, in both cases, these products fail to address the underlying problems and result only in consumers facing new and compounding risks.”

Among various recommendations to the state’s Department of Financial Services, Levine urged regulators to include “all forms of BNPL products” in its pending rules for such lenders, including those that offer rent payment services.

“The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

Ariel Nelson

National Consumer Law Center

Esusu raised $50 million last December. Its platform covers about 5 million rental units, with 12 million people, according to the company’s press release. The company also offers a rent-payment reporting service to help renters build their credit scores. 

Esusu says on its website that its credit services are needed because two-thirds of Americans “live paycheck to paycheck” and that about “30% of lower-income households spend 95% or more of their income on basic necessities like housing, food and utilities.”

Affirm doesn’t allow a consumer to borrow further if they have an outstanding balance from the prior month, Affirm’s vice president of government relations, John Pitts, wrote in a February blog post in response to the Protect Borrowers report, seeking to highlight differences between Affirm and others in the rent market.

“Being financially blindsided by hidden fees and/or still paying January’s rent in March is not solving affordability, it’s stacking debt,” Pitts wrote. “That’s why our products are structurally different.”

Regulators are beginning to “get educated in this space, and they're asking the right questions to provide the consumer protection around it,” said RealPage’s Khoja. Officials in states with the largest numbers of renters – California, Florida, New York and Texas – are among those gathering information about how RNPL firms work, he said.

However, the field of pay later for rent is nascent and state officials are still “catching up” with its growth, said Nelson, the consumer attorney.

“You’re talking about people who are doing whatever it takes to keep a roof over their head,” she said. “This isn’t like I couldn’t pay for an expensive pair of shoes – you could literally be homeless. The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Joe Heck is Zip’s former U.S. CEO. The update also clarifies that Bilt members can earn points without holding a Bilt card.

                Fashion designer Doni Nahmias walks the runway during his menswear show on June 9, 2024 in Los Angeles.
